name: The Walker household — a name from the post office's letter lists
head: walker_george_e

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of 1 July 1834 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1834-07-02, 1 day later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1834-07-01 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1834-07-01 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

basis.note: data/reconstruction/1835_town_model.json#arrival_and_origin.tables.arrival_year_of_the_known_layer, restricted to years at or before 1834.

replaceable_by.match: a dated source that says which year this household came to Chicago

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

reason_for_coming.value: The 1834 season: the harbour works, the opening of the bar and the trade that followed them
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THE SEASON AND NOTHING ELSE. No trade is recorded for this household and no source says why it came; the only thing the evidence gives is when it was here by. This states the draws that were operating in that season and chooses among them nowhere. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

lives_at.note: Not attested: a letter list gives a name and no address.

works_at.note: Not attested. No trade is recorded, so there is no premises to seek.

last_dated_appearance.note: A DATED READING OF THIS PERSON, AND THE LAST ONE THE CORPUS HOLDS. Read from `press_evidence` as `1834-07-02`, which reaches 1834-07-02 — 364 day(s) short of 1835-07-01. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Nothing after 1834-07-16 follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap.

persons.name: George E. Walker

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. A list of uncalled-for letters prints a name and no trade, and this pass will not read one in.

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'George E. Walker 2' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 33, reprinted over 3 consecutive issues — dated 1834-07-02 to 1834-07-16. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

resident_research.summary: A primary 1835 Illinois legislative/land record identifies George E. Walker near Utica; the exact name is strong but competing geography prevents a Chicago identity assertion.

merge_ruling.for_merge: Both are Georges in chicago_democrat_1833_1835 and the town holds no third Walker of that forename. Kept verbatim from T-0839 so the argument survives its refusal.
merge_ruling.against_merge: EACH MIDDLE INITIAL IS PRINTED TWICE, BY INDEPENDENT HANDS. George E. Walker is 'George E. Walker' in the Democrat's letter list of 2 July 1834 and 'Walker, George E.' in Fergus's old-settler death notice of 9 November 1874. George H. Walker is 'WALKER, GEORGE H' on the 1832 Black Hawk enrollment roll and 'G. H. Walker' in the Democrat's letter list of 1 April 1834. A copyist's mis-set is the WHOLE ground for folding a contradicted middle initial, and it does not survive two independent attestations on each side: four printings, two sources apiece, E twice and H twice. The town's other Walker cards are James and Jeremiah. T-0480's research adds, without asserting it, a George E. Walker in an 1835 Illinois land record near Utica — competing geography, recorded and not leaned on.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white males 20 under 30', one of its male bands, conditioned on `named_on_a_roll_15_and_over` because the person is named in their own right on any other roll this layer was minted from - a letter list, a subscription, a court docket, a trade notice - or carries a role, a trade, a marriage or a parenthood.

replaceable_by.match: a source that states this person's age, their birth year, or an interval either can be read out of

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('walker_george_e:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: A FORENAME THAT STANDS IN ONE SEX'S NAMING ONLY. 'George' is read as male because 2 persons in this layer whose sex a source records bear it (dole_george_w, snow_george_w), and it stands in the yankee male forename pool of this town's own attested naming. Nothing about this person is recorded; the name is the whole of the reasoning, and the table that licenses it — data/research/residents/forename_sex.json — refuses a name its own evidence splits, refuses Jean, Marion, Leslie and Francis by name, and refuses an initial outright.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

surname_collision.refusal: the town already names a Walker
surname_collision.note: A COLLISION SAID, NOT ACTED ON. Run against the tree as it stands, this pass would not MINT this card: refusal 7 — 'the town already names a Walker' — lands on it, because George H Walker (hh_walker_george_h); James Walker (hh_walker_james); Jeremiah Walker (hh_walker_jeremiah) already holds the family name Walker. The owner ruled on 2026-09-18 (T-0660, option (c)) that refusals 7 and 8 are MINT-TIME rules: they decide whether a new household may be minted on a family name the town already spends, and they do not un-mint one that already stands. So this record is not retired, its id is not redirected at anybody, the town's population does not move, and the research row and directory matches it carries are not stranded on a retirement nothing draws. What has changed is that the collision is legible: a reader sees both cards and why both are here. REFUSAL 7 IS NOT A CLAIM THAT TWO RECORDS ARE ONE PERSON — it is the precedence rule between this pass and the ones above it, which give a man the papers gave a trade the family name a letter list only spells. Two of the collisions this reading uncovered are two different men. The pass's `rank()` is unchanged and the cohort is not re-derived; that was option (b)'s cost and the ruling declined to pay it. The derivation behind this block, both readings side by side, is docs/RESEARCH/letter-list-surname-collisions.md.
